primary_claim: Single-layer LoRA finetuning on insecure code is sufficient to induce emergent misalignment in Qwen2.5-Coder-32B-Instruct, and steering vectors extracted from those LoRAs can partially replicate the misaligned behavior in the un-finetuned model (correlated direction and behavior), though not well enough to conclude that emergent misalignment reduces to a single steering vector at one layer.

effect.value: Strong emergent misalignment for single-layer LoRA at layers 21 and 41, moderate at layer 31, none at layer 51; example layer-21 (r=32) response scored 2.3/100 alignment, 26.7/100 coherence; steered (non-finetuned) models show similar coherence/alignment distributions to LoRA-finetuned models but require much higher scaling to match

contradicts_or_qualifies: Qualifies the 'evil direction' hypothesis speculated after the original Emergent Misalignment paper: results suggest that if such a direction exists, it is unlikely to be a single vector and instead may rely on multiple layers
stated_future_work: Further analysis of the steering vectors produced, and the changes in these vectors across layers and their dynamics when trained and steered
Finetuning other layers, trying more values of r in the LoRA, and testing other α values
Understanding why specific α values push the model into high incoherence (norm of steering vector vs. activation norm, or other factors)
limitations_stated: Due to cost and resource constraints, only layers 21, 31, 41, 51 (of 64 total) were tested; better layers may exist outside this range
GPT-4o judge scores show rounding artifacts, so raw scores can be misleading and required manual verification of true misalignment
Steering vector effect is noisy/imperfect — matching LoRA-level misalignment with a steering vector requires a higher α that leaves the model less coherent than the LoRA
Layer 51's vector showed promising cosine similarity but did not exhibit misalignment when used to steer
quote: Single-layer LoRAs are sufficient to induce emergent misalignment.
